analysis: Palula práaču ‘guest’ has early long root prominence before u. The independently reconstructed yaka extension and guest-reception semantics justify placing it among extended nouns, but the root vowel is historically long and the whole input's accent is unknown. Related prā́rtha cannot automatically donate its accent to this formation.
unresolved: Verify the male/female guest paradigm and the rthya cluster development.

analysis: Gilgit phar- and phar b- contain a short unaccented root citation, the latter in a light-verb construction. The proposed relation to phir- under 9078 concerns root alternation and does not establish a unique old accent. Bare stems and whole constructions must not be counted as contrasting accent outcomes.
unresolved: Recover inflected marked forms and distinguish simple from light-verb uses.

input: *phālgu, distinct from corrupt broad headword pǹalgu
analysis: Palula phaág/Strand phâʹg and Gilgit phaág agree on late aa. The immediate input is independently the long *phālgu branch, not the corrupt broad headword pǹalgu. Turner original cached page 509 confirms branch 2 *phālgu and an addendum reading phalgu for branch 1; the apparent grave on n is not usable old accent. Shina phăgí adds a short-root, final-accent plural.
unresolved: Inspect the original scan for the corrupt headword and recover the fig paradigm; compare singular late aa with plural shortening.

analysis: Gilgit phéeri ‘whirlpool’ has early long root prominence before i and belongs to the nominal turn formation, whereas the turn/return verbs and ‘again’ adverbs contain other suffixes. The broad family also includes a causative. These independently different formations cannot supply one pooled accent outcome.
unresolved: Assign immediate formation and grammatical cell to each record and inspect the whirlpool noun's declension.

analysis: Palula phúngu, Gilgit phúṅe/phú~e, Kohistani phúgo and Astori phúṅi retain short-root prominence before differing endings. Guresi phúu~ṅɨ has early long quantity, plausibly tied to nasal or cluster history. The source rejects a simple *spaṁśuka derivation, so no accent should be imported from śmáśru. Endings and nasal retention provide independent comparison variables.
unresolved: Determine number/gender of the endings and whether Guresi length accompanies nasal weakening.

analysis: Palula phútu ‘fly’ has initial short-root prominence before u; older phutto and phutti ‘mosquito’ preserve different gender or diminutive endings. The semantic extension from smallness to insects is plausible, but an expressive unaccented root cannot test old-accent preservation. Fly and mosquito must retain their lexical distinction.
unresolved: Check insect species and the productive gender/diminutive pattern.

analysis: Palula phéepi has early long prominence before the feminine ending, while Strand phʹôpo denotes the aunt's husband and shows a different vowel and masculine ending. These are a useful gender pair, not variants of one aunt form. Kalkoti pheep is explicitly in Liljegren 2013's low-rising glottalized class; its segment-only token is not toneless.
unresolved: Compare the kinship paradigms and assess the aspiration-plus-final-vowel history in Kalkoti.

analysis: Palula pháapu/Strand phʹâpu has early long root prominence despite an aspirated onset, illustrating why aspiration alone is not a universal late-accent rule. It is a vowel-final expressive body-part noun, not a closed monosyllable. Sawi phapusḗ and pā́pus differ in suffix retention and accent position, requiring source and grammatical-cell separation.
unresolved: Read Sawi forms in context and compare number and suffix variants; do not force one proto-accent onto the expressive set.

analysis: Gilgit phúu th- has an early long ideophonic component in a light-verb construction. The old source already permits long and short expressive variants. Its prosody and length are therefore not directly comparable to inherited nominal root accent, though the construction is historically and semantically transparent.
unresolved: Verify independent versus phrase-level prominence of the ideophone.

analysis: Palula phuukíi accents the verbal citation ending, while the old form contains additional tka material related to the blowing ideophone. The modern long root is not the accented component in this citation. Comparison with 9101 requires both derivation and grammatical-cell controls.
unresolved: Recover imperative and perfective forms and establish the tka cluster development.

analysis: Gilgit ban- ‘put on clothes’ is a short bare stem, not the noun bandhá ‘bond’. The independently accented causative is a different old formation. Clothing semantics do not disrupt the bind connection, but no mora outcome can be extracted from the unmarked root alone.
unresolved: Read the inflected paradigm and distinguish simple bind from causative and clothing constructions.

analysis: Palula bakaraál/Strand bakarâʹl has late aa in the final component, whereas early long agent payáa~lo retains an ending. The independent goat-plus-keeper compound and final-vowel loss motivate separate comparison. Accents of bárkara and pālá are constituent evidence, not a supplied accent for the reconstructed whole.
unresolved: Compare keeper compounds with and without final vowels and recover plural or oblique cells.

analysis: Kohistani, Guresi and Astori láa show early aa after severe reduction, while Chilas lāgo retains extra material. The source relates bahura to bahulá and bahú but does not mark the immediate form's accent. Quantifier inflection, r/l history and contraction are independent considerations before treating early aa as accent reversal.
unresolved: Check exact derivation and the grammatical status of lāgo versus láa.

analysis: Palula báabu has early aa, Gilgit and Astori baábo late aa, and Kohistani bubáa final aa. This is a real cross-language morphological and mora difference within a nursery kin term. The unaccented expressive input provides no deterministic inherited-accent prediction; kinship declension and vocative reshaping are concrete alternatives to examine. Kalkoti bab is short.
unresolved: Compare singular, vocative and plural forms before attributing the difference to an accent law.

analysis: Strand bhâyʹûṛi ‘sleeve’ has prominence in the long final root component before i; older bhayū́ṛi means bracelet. Arm plus ornament supports the semantic extension, but the compound and its feminine ending distinguish it from either constituent alone. The first sequence ay must not be treated mechanically as two vowel nuclei.
unresolved: Check the sleeve versus bracelet lexical relation and the source's compound segmentation and mora notation.

analysis: Palula beeṭí/Strand bêṭʹi has final short-i accent after an unaccented long root. This is a genuine boundary to a universal root-accented i-noun rule. The immediate bēṭṭa variant and juvenile-animal formation are independent of the observed accent; the broad ‘defective’ gloss is too loose to establish a unique historical derivation.
unresolved: Read lamb age/gender and declension and evaluate the lexical family on segmental and semantic evidence.

analysis: Palula bhúuru ‘deaf’ has early long root prominence before u, but buuḍóolu ‘spider’ accents a later extended root syllable; Gilgit taṛabúulo has still more material. These are distinct formations within a loose expressive family. The deaf lexeme is also linked under 9530 and 9633 and must not count three times.
unresolved: Compare competing deaf inputs and parse the spider extensions and any compound components.

analysis: Palula búuḍu/Strand bʹûḍo has early long root prominence before the gender ending. Turner explicitly argues that initial b across languages excludes direct derivation from vr̥ddhá and offers contamination or a br̥h-related alternative. Importing vr̥ddhá's accent to create a late-to-early exception would ignore that independent segmental objection.
unresolved: Retain the two stated old alternatives and compare animate gender inflection and cluster reduction.

analysis: Gilgit boṛiǰ- ‘sink’ is a passive/intransitive formation, while boṛ- ‘ache in shoulder and neck’ may reflect a semantic or lexical extension. Older forms include causative ‘make sink’. All are bare or differently suffixed citations, and the expressive root family offers no unique old accent.
unresolved: Read the ache sense and distinguish causative versus passive paradigms before grouping outcomes.

analysis: Palula búǰa/Biori búǰe are present or imperative dictionary forms with short-root accent, while older búddo and Shina budo are participial or adjectival formations. A graph link through buddha does not make the modern understand lemma a direct phonological reflex of the old participle. The palatal and dental stems independently reveal the cell difference.
unresolved: Recover complete understand/wake paradigms and classify the old participial reflex separately.

analysis: Palula bhun ‘down’ is a short local element. The longer bhunaṛo/bhunaṛā forms add morphology, and finger names such as bhunimi aṅgúṛi place prominence in a compound member. Related budhná is accented but not identical to the metathesized immediate input. The grammatical and compound uses must be separated from a free bottom noun.
unresolved: Read the local paradigm and parse the finger-name compounds.

analysis: Palula bhus/Strand bhʹus is a short monosyllable, so the aspirated onset does not produce a long-mora opposition here. Turner discusses competing expressive and borrowing connections rather than a secure accented old input. The straw meaning is close to chaff and does not itself require a new etymology.
unresolved: Check whether any paradigm cell lengthens the root and assess the source's explicit origin alternatives.

analysis: Strand buṛʹûko ‘bud’ has early long prominence on an extended final root syllable before o. The added uka material independently motivates a derived plant-unit class. The source compares Persian bōta, so donor adaptation is a possibility requiring evidence, not an inherited Sanskrit accent to assume.
unresolved: Compare the uka derivative and documented plant-loan forms and recover inflection.

analysis: Strand burʹa ‘sawdust’ accents final short a and has a shortened root relative to the reconstruction. This is not a root-accented u/o noun and should remain in a final-a nominal class if the form is a singular rather than an oblique. Powder-to-sawdust semantics are straightforward but old accent is unknown.
unresolved: Read the source's grammatical label and paradigm to identify the final-a cell.

analysis: Gilgit and Astori bréspat have initial short prominence after contraction. The old deity name has two accents in the database, so the review label ‘unaccented’ is misleading. Compound prosody and possible learned or regional transmission of weekday names must be established; this is not a simple single-accent inherited noun.
unresolved: Verify historical double-accent notation and the source of the weekday vocabulary.

analysis: Guresi brestvaár accents late aa in the day component, contrasting structurally with Gilgit bréspat under 9303, which lacks vāra. The added day constituent independently explains why the accent sites differ. The whole compound's old accent and transmission remain unknown.
unresolved: Check whether Guresi preserves both constituent prominences and compare its other vāra weekdays.

analysis: Gilgit and Astori bóodo show early oo before final o, the reflex of old au in a derivative relating to Mercury. The accent of parent budhá does not determine the vr̥ddhi derivative baudha, whose accent is unmarked here. Weekday transmission and nominal adaptation must be controlled before adding this to inherited noun statistics.
unresolved: Compare the weekday set and check whether this is a borrowed or inherited derivative.

analysis: Palula bhakúlu has short prominence on the final root syllable before u and an independently visible ul extension. Kohistani bhaák ‘bull’ instead has late aa in a closed monosyllable, compatible with a new-long aspirated environment but not directly the same formation. Lump-to-fat and lump-to-bull are separate semantic derivations.
unresolved: Verify the bull etymology and compare the adjective's gender endings and the bull's quantity history.

analysis: Palula bheéṇ/Strand bhêʹṇ has late ee after contraction and final-vowel loss. Kalkoti bään belongs to the explicitly low-level set in Liljegren 2013. The old feminine formation and multiple medial-loss stages independently distinguish it from a simple long-root noun; neither parent bhága nor bhagín can be assigned as its accent without argument.
unresolved: Trace feminine contraction and compare sister inflection and aspiration history across sources.

analysis: Palula bhanǰóo/Biori bhanǰúu accent the citation ending; ‘play an instrument’ extends the beat sense. The old present has independently different strong and weak stem shapes and accented endings. A single reconstructed lemma therefore cannot supply the prediction for every modern cell.
unresolved: Compare matched person/tense forms, including older bhanǰū́m, and separate root from ending accent.

analysis: Palula babaáy and Strand babâʹy place late prominence on final aa before y; Biori babéi and Sawi bōbái have corresponding final diphthongal forms. The expressive or reconstructed input has no marked accent, and the repeated initial syllable plus y require a formation history. These forms are not inherited long monosyllables.
unresolved: Read the fruit paradigm and determine whether final y reflects the feminine or another nominal extension.

analysis: Gilgit báage th- has early long prominence on the nominal part of ‘distribute’, whereas Palula bhaagíi accents the verb's citation ending. Old ‘divisible’ and substantive ‘part’ are related derivations, so the noun/light-verb construction and simple verb cannot be treated as one accent cell. The root's long quantity is independently inherited.
unresolved: Recover the free share noun and the divide paradigm and identify the immediate ya formation.

analysis: Palula bhaanóoṛ/bhaaṇóol and Strand bhâṇʹôl have early long prominence on the final root component after substantial contraction. The old storage-building compound supports a shed or pasture-hut semantic development. The r/l variants and goat-house compound need separation; this is not a simple accent retention case from either constituent.
unresolved: Trace the g-loss contraction and compare shed inflection and the r/l dialect variants.

analysis: Palula bharíiw/Biori bharéew and Strand bharʹîw have early long prominence in the contracted final component; Gilgit baráo retains a different vowel sequence. The old wife-plus-keeper reconstruction and bhāryā's svarita require compound analysis. Kalkoti bärä is segmentally informative but its tone cannot be inferred from absent accents.
unresolved: Verify the compound derivation and vowel sequence interpretation and recover comparable kinship cells.

analysis: Palula bhóo/Biori bhúu is an early long monosyllabic modal citation, whereas the old causative means cause to be, cherish or consider. Semantic grammaticalization and contraction are independent reasons for a special verbal class. Strand's bare bh- and Sawi buw do not provide comparable mora readings.
unresolved: Check modal inflection and the historical causative-to-ability argument.

analysis: Gilgit báaṣ has early aa, contrasting with baáṣ ‘armpit’ from vákṣas despite near segmental identity. The speech word has independently old long ā, whereas armpit has new length after cluster reduction. This is a valuable chronology control even though bhāṣā's old accent is unmarked. Older baṣ also requires dialect and quantity caution.
unresolved: Verify the two minimal-pair entries and whether the older short form reflects source convention or real shortening.

analysis: Palula bhit/Strand bhʹit is a short monosyllable, with older bhittu/bhitta retaining endings. The split-timber meaning independently supports the derivation, and final-vowel variation offers a historical control. An aspirated onset alone clearly does not ensure long quantity or late mora accent.
unresolved: Check whether the older endings are citation or inflectional forms and recover the current plank paradigm.

analysis: Palula bhíia/Biori bhíie retains early prominence on ii before the final vowel, whereas Gilgit biǰ- has shortening and a palatal consonant. The y-bearing formation and imperative endings distinguish this from closed h-initial nouns. Old accent is not supplied, but the modern early long verbal outcome is explicit.
unresolved: Read the imperative and present paradigms and establish the ii-plus-vowel syllabification.

analysis: Strand bhʹoči has short initial prominence before i; Sawi boiču has a different vowel sequence and ending. The immediate long-o variant and loose ‘defective’ root family do not provide an independently accented input. Genital expressive vocabulary and gender formation require lexical evidence before any more precise reconstruction.
unresolved: Read the source's semantic and segmental argument and compare the Sawi ending.

analysis: Palula bhúuru has early long prominence before u and is the same deaf lexeme also grouped under 9268 and 9633. The different reconstructed roots are alternatives within a broad defective-word family, not independent supporting cases. The modern adjective can be classified morphologically while historical input uncertainty remains explicit.
unresolved: Assess the competing consonant and aspiration histories without choosing by accent fit.

analysis: Gilgit buyá~l/bu~yá~l and Guresi mu~yál accent the final short root syllable. Nasalization and initial b/m variation distinguish the contracted earth compound from Palula's longer bhūmicala formation under 9560. The accent of parent bhū́ alone does not fix the compound's old accent.
unresolved: Compare the bhū versus bhūmi compounds and source treatment of final nasalized vowel length.

analysis: Strand ghumâʹl has late final aa. Turner original cached page 545 says Palula ghōmāl/ghūmāl/gahumāl mean earthquake and may be deformed after ghōm/ghuma ‘wheat’ to avoid ill-luck. The database incorrectly propagated ‘wheat’ onto the earthquake forms and included the comparison nouns as reflexes. The source's contamination proposal explains unusual gh independently of accent, but remains explicitly tentative.
unresolved: Verify the taboo proposal against later descriptions; retain earthquake gloss corrections and exclude wheat comparators from this family count.

analysis: Palula bhrʹuǰ is short after metathesis, while Buddruss Gilgit juúṣ ‘bark’ and joóẓi ‘tree’ have late long vowels. Degener ǰuẓ is short/unmarked, creating a source or lexical-cell issue. The au derivative and tree-versus-bark distinction are independent variables; the modern forms do not prove a single old accent.
unresolved: Verify Degener and Buddruss entries and assign bark versus tree and bhūrja versus bhaurja separately.

analysis: Strand bhʹûro has early long root prominence and agrees with Liljegren bhúuru. This is the same modern adjective linked to defective roots under 9268 and 9530. The rhotic input may reduce the consonantal derivation required, but it is a reconstructed alternative and cannot be preferred solely because its vowel fits the modern form.
unresolved: Compare independent regional cognates and the source's relationships among bhōra, bhōḍa and bhōla.

analysis: Guresi bóṅu vaár retains separately marked prominence in both constituents, including late aa in ‘day’. This cannot be flattened into a single lexical accent token. The vr̥ddhi planet adjective and day compound also belong to culturally transmitted weekday vocabulary, with unknown whole-word old accent.
unresolved: Preserve component-level readings and compare Guresi weekday construction prosody.

analysis: Palula bhraaǰái/bhraaǰéi accents the final diphthong, while Shina jajeé and Kohistani jaẓá show different contractions and endings. The compound independently contains jāyā́, but its whole old accent is not supplied. Kinship relation labels also differ by speaker gender and must be retained rather than pooled.
unresolved: Check kinship definitions and paradigms and resolve diphthong versus hiatus in each transcription.

analysis: Strand bhrâpʹutr places short prominence in the son component after an unaccented long first component. The compound structure independently distinguishes it from free brother or son nouns. Constituent accents bhrā́tr̥ and putrá are relevant but do not supply the accent of the entire historical compound.
unresolved: Read compound and kinship inflection and whether any secondary prominence is recorded.

analysis: Gilgit bram- is a short bare stem despite one old variant's long root; the source also records a short old variant. The causative morphology and vowel alternatives must be established before shortening is inferred. No modern accent is explicitly marked in the citation.
unresolved: Extract marked paradigm cells and identify the relevant long versus short old causative variant.

analysis: Palula bhaṛíi accents the verb's citation ending, while the old input is an instrument noun or adjective. Turner explicitly proposes eastern Middle Indo-Aryan *bhāṭha but notes the absence of expected medial aspiration. This is an existing segmental problem, not a new accent exception; the modern verb may be denominal.
unresolved: Read the verb's derivational status and paradigm and retain the source's aspiration caveat.

input: ma base; mā́m, máyā, máhyam, máma, enclitic mē
analysis: Palula máa- versus short ma and Strand mʹa occurs across direct and other pronominal uses, while Shina ma/mas/mei and other languages preserve different cases. The broad unaccented base conceals independently accented old case forms and enclitics. Pronoun accent must therefore be compared by case and clitic status, never as a single noun-like outcome.
unresolved: Construct matched pronoun paradigms and determine the source's meaning of the long bound máa- form.
